ei.title: From Data to Insight: The Power of Visualization

fullPassage: The emergence of the social sciences in the nineteenth century and the ability to work with large datasets created demand for new ways of visualizing information. Processed numerical information was best expressed in tables, charts, and graphs. Mathematics, natural sciences, and social sciences that employed statistics were at the (a) forefront of the development of charts and graphs. History was a consumer, not a designer, of most of these new visualizations—and mostly a sparing consumer at that, since economic and social history lagged behind political history as an area of research. Simple charts and graphs were not difficult to interpret, and their visual conventions became part of what any (b) ordinary reader would be expected to follow. As statistical analysis became more (c) sophisticated, the visualizations that resulted became more and more central to the argument. In some cases, the visualization made interpretation possible. These success stories (d) demonstrated the worth of statistical analysis and visualization. Perhaps the most notable example is John Snow's map of the incidence of cholera in an 1854 London outbreak, which helped plot the source of the outbreak at a single water pump in the neighborhood. Snow's cholera map showed that visualizations could serve as both narrative and analysis. Authors began to experiment with ways of using visual clues to tell complex stories about events, increasing the amount of information that could be conveyed in a small space and thereby (e) intensifying the limitations of two dimensions in print.

questions.passage: The emergence of the social sciences in the nineteenth century and the ability to work with large datasets ①<u>created</u> demand for new ways of visualizing information. Mathematics and social sciences that ②<u>employed</u> statistics were at the forefront. Simple charts were not difficult ③<u>interpreting</u>, and their conventions became part of what any reader would be expected ④<u>to follow</u>.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: ③ interpreting → to interpret: 'difficult to + 동사원형' 구문이다.
det.analysis:
✅ ① created: 복합 주어(emergence and ability) + 과거동사 정상
✅ ② employed: 관계절 동사 정상
❌ ③ interpreting: difficult + to부정사 (not difficult to interpret)
✅ ④ to follow: be expected to + 동사원형 정상
det.tip: be difficult to + 동사원형 (to부정사의 형용사적 용법)

questions.passage: As statistical analysis became more sophisticated, the visualizations ①<u>that</u> resulted became more central to the argument. Perhaps the most notable example is Snow's map of the incidence of cholera, ②<u>which</u> helped plot the source. Authors began to experiment with ways of ③<u>using</u> visual clues, ④<u>increasing</u> the amount of information that could be conveyed.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: 모두 어법상 올바르다. ① that: 주격 관계대명사, ② which: 계속적 용법 관계대명사, ③ using: 전치사 of + 동명사, ④ increasing: 분사구문 (결과)
det.analysis:
✅ ① that: 주격 관계대명사 (the visualizations that resulted)
✅ ② which: 계속적 용법 (map, which helped)
✅ ③ using: of + 동명사
✅ ④ increasing: 분사구문
det.tip: 이 문제는 모두 올바른 어법 — 함정 문제
